questions.question: For the system $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t+\boldsymbol{b}$ with a real $n\times n$ matrix $A$ and constant $\boldsymbol{b}$, which condition is equivalent to the equilibrium being asymptotically stable (every solution converges to it)?
options: Every eigenvalue of $A$, real or complex, has $\lvert\lambda\rvert<1$.
Every entry of $A$ satisfies $\lvert a_{ij}\rvert<1$.
Every real eigenvalue of $A$ lies strictly between $-1$ and $1$.
All eigenvalues of $A$ lie in the closed disc $\lvert\lambda\rvert\le1$.

questions.question: For $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t+\boldsymbol{b}$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&1\\1&0.5\end{pmatrix}$, a student argues the equilibrium is asymptotically stable because both diagonal entries equal $0.5$. Is this right?
options: Yes: diagonal entries below $1$ are the eigenvalues here.
Yes: all entries have absolute value at most $1$.
No: the eigenvalues are $1.5$ and $-0.5$, so it is unstable.
No: the off-diagonal entry $1$ is itself an eigenvalue.

questions.question: The real matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1.2\\1.2&0\end{pmatrix}$ has no real eigenvalues. What does this mean for the stability of $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t$?
options: Stable: no real eigenvalue lies outside $(-1,1)$.
Undecided: the criterion applies only to real eigenvalues.
Stable: the eigenvalues $\pm1.2\mathrm{i}$ have real part $0$.
Unstable: its eigenvalues $\pm1.2\mathrm{i}$ have modulus $1.2>1$.

questions.question: For $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t+\boldsymbol{b}$ with $I-A$ invertible, the constant vector $\boldsymbol{b}$ is multiplied by $10$. How does this affect the equilibrium and its stability?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is unchanged; stability may be lost as $\boldsymbol{b}$ grows.
$\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is multiplied by $10$; stability is unchanged.
$\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is multiplied by $10$; the eigenvalues of $A$ grow with it.
$\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is multiplied by $10$; stability now needs $\lvert\lambda\rvert<0.1$.

questions.question: Is the equilibrium of $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t+\boldsymbol{b}$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}0.6&5\\0&-0.9\end{pmatrix}$ asymptotically stable?
options: Yes: $A$ is triangular with eigenvalues $0.6$ and $-0.9$.
No: the entry $5$ makes the powers $A^t$ grow without bound.
No: the eigenvalue $-0.9$ is negative, so solutions oscillate away.
Yes, but only if the entry $5$ is replaced by a number below $1$.

questions.question: For $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t+\boldsymbol{b}$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0\\0&0.2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}=(1,4)^{\top}$, what is the equilibrium $\boldsymbol{x}^*$?
For $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0\\0&-1.1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{x}_0=(1,1)^{\top}$, how does $\boldsymbol{x}_t$ behave?
options: Both components converge to $0$, since $0.9-1.1<0$.
The first component decays; the second alternates and grows.
Both components grow, since one eigenvalue lies outside the unit circle.
The second component decays while alternating, as $-1.1$ is negative.

questions.question: For $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}0.8&-0.8\\0.8&0.8\end{pmatrix}$, eigenvalues $0.8\pm0.8\mathrm{i}$, how do solutions behave?
options: They spiral outwards: $\lvert\lambda\rvert=0.8\sqrt{2}\approx1.13>1$.
They spiral inwards: the real part $0.8$ is below $1$.
They spiral inwards: every entry has absolute value $0.8$.
They rotate with constant size: the eigenvalues are nonreal.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&2\\-0.5&1\end{pmatrix}$, use $\lvert\det A\rvert=\prod_i\lvert\lambda_i\rvert$ to decide whether $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t$ can be asymptotically stable.
options: Not stable: $\det A=1.5$ forces some $\lvert\lambda\rvert>1$.
It is stable: $\det A=-0.5$, below $1$ in absolute value.
It is stable: $\lvert\det A\rvert>1$ is necessary for stability.
No conclusion: $\det A$ says nothing about stability.

questions.question: For a real $3\times3$ matrix $A$ with $\lvert\det A\rvert=0.5$, what follows about the stability of $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t$?
options: It is stable: $\lvert\det A\rvert<1$ is necessary and sufficient.
It is stable: the $2\times2$ test passes once $\lvert\det A\rvert<1$.
It is unstable: a $3\times3$ matrix needs $\lvert\det A\rvert<\tfrac{1}{3}$.
Nothing: $\operatorname{diag}(2,0.5,0.5)$ has $\det A=0.5$ yet is unstable.

questions.question: Suppose every eigenvalue of $A$ satisfies $\lvert\lambda\rvert<1$. Why does $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t+\boldsymbol{b}$ then have exactly one equilibrium $\boldsymbol{x}^*$?
options: $A$ is invertible, so $\boldsymbol{x}^*=A^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}$.
$A^t\to O$ makes $\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{0}$ the only option.
$1$ is not an eigenvalue, so $I-A$ is invertible.
All entries of $I-A$ are then positive.

questions.question: For $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&0.5\end{pmatrix}$, the solution from $\boldsymbol{x}_0=(0,3)^{\top}$ is $(0,3\cdot0.5^t)^{\top}\to\boldsymbol{0}$. Is $\boldsymbol{0}$ asymptotically stable?
options: Yes: one convergent solution shows that $A^t\to O$.
Yes: the eigenvalue $0.5$ of the starting direction is below $1$.
No: the solution from $(0,3)^{\top}$ does not actually converge.
No: any start with nonzero first component grows like $2^t$.

questions.question: Apply the $2\times2$ test ($\lvert\det A\rvert<1$ and $\lvert\operatorname{tr}A\rvert<1+\det A$) to $A=\begin{pmatrix}0.2&0.5\\0.4&0.3\end{pmatrix}$. What is the conclusion?
options: Unstable: $\det A=-0.14$ is negative.
Undecided: the test is valid only for triangular $A$.
Asymptotically stable: $\lvert-0.14\rvert<1$ and $0.5<0.86$.
Unstable: $\lvert\operatorname{tr}A\rvert=0.5$ exceeds $\lvert\det A\rvert$.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}0.8&1\\0&0.8\end{pmatrix}$ (not diagonalisable), $A^t=\begin{pmatrix}0.8^t&t\,0.8^{t-1}\\0&0.8^t\end{pmatrix}$. Is $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t$ asymptotically stable?
options: No: the factor $t$ makes the top-right entry grow.
Yes: $t\,0.8^{t-1}\to0$, so $A^t\to O$.
No: a non-diagonalisable matrix is never stable.
No: the entry $1$ is not below $1$ in absolute value.

questions.question: For $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t+\boldsymbol{b}$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.5\\0&0.5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}=(1,1)^{\top}$, what is the equilibrium that every solution approaches?

For $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.2\\0.1&0.8\end{pmatrix}$ (eigenvalues $1$ and $0.7$), every solution converges. Why is $\boldsymbol{0}$ not asymptotically stable?
options: Limits are multiples of $(2,1)^{\top}$ that depend on $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.
It is: every solution converges, which is the definition.
The eigenvalue $0.7$ makes solutions oscillate around $\boldsymbol{0}$.
Solutions grow along $(2,1)^{\top}$, since the eigenvalue $1$ is not below $1$.

questions.question: The equation $x_{t+2}+a_1x_{t+1}+a_0x_t=b$ has companion matrix $C=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-a_0&-a_1\end{pmatrix}$. What does the test $\lvert\det C\rvert<1$, $\lvert\operatorname{tr}C\rvert<1+\det C$ become?
options: $\lvert a_0\rvert<1$ and $\lvert a_1\rvert<1-a_0$
$\lvert a_1\rvert<1$ and $\lvert a_0\rvert<1+a_1$
$\lvert a_0\rvert<1$ and $a_1<1+a_0$, no modulus
$\lvert a_0\rvert<1$ and $\lvert a_1\rvert<1+a_0$

questions.question: For $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t+\boldsymbol{b}$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&k\\k&0.5\end{pmatrix}$ and real $k$, the eigenvalues are $0.5+k$ and $0.5-k$. For which $k$ is the equilibrium asymptotically stable?
options: Exactly for $-\tfrac{3}{2}<k<\tfrac{1}{2}$
Exactly for $-\tfrac{1}{2}<k<\tfrac{1}{2}$
Exactly for $-1<k<1$
Exactly for $0\le k<\tfrac{1}{2}$

questions.question: For $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0.5\\2&0\end{pmatrix}$, which conclusion about the zero equilibrium is correct?
options: Asymptotically stable: both diagonal entries are $0$.
Unbounded solutions: the entry $2$ exceeds $1$.
Asymptotically stable: $\lvert\operatorname{tr}A\rvert=0<1+\det A$.
Not asymptotically stable: eigenvalues are $\pm1$, and $A^2=I$.

questions.question: A real $2\times2$ matrix $A$ has eigenvalues $\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\pi/3}$. How do nonzero solutions of $\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t$ behave?
options: They spiral into $\boldsymbol{0}$, since the real parts equal $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
They are bounded, repeat after $6$ steps and never reach $\boldsymbol{0}$.
They spiral outwards, since $\lvert\lambda\rvert=1$ is not below $1$.
They converge to a nonzero limit fixed by $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.
